Assiniboine

Assiniboine is an outside name for northern Plains peoples who use names including Nakoda, Nakota and Nakona in community contexts. Their histories and kinship cross the Canada–United States border, while contemporary governments remain distinct. Fort Belknap, Fort Peck and Saskatchewan First Nations offer different perspectives on land, language and continuing political life.

Names & relationshipsAssiniboine/Nakoda is not one government. Aaniiih/Gros Ventre at Fort Belknap and Dakota at Fort Peck are distinct co-resident peoples. Stoney Nakoda has close historical and linguistic relationships, but a Nakoda spelling alone does not identify the same community, language variety or government.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Names, language and origin accounts

Fort Belknap’s history identifies Assiniboine people as Nakoda or Nakota. Assiniboine derives from an Ojibwe name associated with cooking with heated stones. These names should be read in their local contexts. Linguistically, Nakoda belongs to the Siouan family. Linda Cumberland’s grammar also cautions against an old classification that treated Nakoda simply as a minor variant of Dakota and Lakota. Linguistic relationships do not settle every question of historical origin: Fort Belknap preserves oral accounts that differ from familiar outsider migration narratives.

Read the sources [1] Fort Belknap Indian Community [6] University of Nebraska Press / JSTOR

02

Bison, mobility and trade networks

Bison supplied food, hides and materials for mobile Plains communities. Assiniboine people also traded meat and pelts with Missouri River agricultural communities for crops and other goods. Their relations with European trading companies built on Indigenous knowledge, diplomacy and exchange. At Fort Union, founded in 1828, Assiniboine permission enabled the post’s establishment, and Assiniboine traders became its principal partners. Women’s marriages and kinship relationships helped sustain those connections. This history places Indigenous communities at the center of the trading economy rather than at its margins.

Read the sources [2] National Park Service / Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site

03

Epidemics and the coercion of reservation life

Smallpox repeatedly devastated northern Plains communities, including Assiniboine people connected with the Upper Missouri trade. The University of Saskatchewan’s synthesis places these epidemics alongside changing commercial networks and the destruction of bison herds. It describes later reserve life as shaped by restricted mobility, hunger, residential schooling and prohibitions on cultural and political activities. These pressures differed across the international boundary and among local communities. Reservation settlement consequently cannot be explained as a simple voluntary abandonment of older lifeways or as the end of Indigenous collective identity.

Read the sources [2] National Park Service / Fort Union Trading Post National Historic Site [7] Gladue Rights Research Database / University of Saskatchewan

04

Carry the Kettle and Cypress Hills homelands

FHQ Developments’ community account dates the Treaty 4 adhesion by ancestors of Carry the Kettle to September 25, 1877 at Fort Walsh. It identifies the western Cypress Hills, including the Head of the Mountain, as a homeland of enduring significance. The community-authored history Owóknage follows forced removal from those lands to the area south of Sintaluta, Saskatchewan. Its published contents bring together land use, treaty-era farming, language, sacred places, harvesting and environmental concerns, drawing on Elder interviews as well as documentary research.

Read the sources [3] FHQ Developments [4] Carry the Kettle First Nation / University of Regina Press

05

Distinct peoples within contemporary governments

Fort Belknap Indian Community in Montana unites Nakoda and Aaniiih, also called Gros Ventre, in a shared government. The reservation was established in 1888 and represents only part of the peoples’ wider ancestral territories. Fort Peck institutions separately serve Assiniboine and Sioux communities; their language department distinguishes Nakona/Nakoda from Dakota. Carry the Kettle is another particular First Nation rather than a name for all Assiniboine people in Canada. Shared institutions, broad peoplehood and individual governments therefore need to be kept distinct when tracing contemporary sovereignty.

Read the sources [1] Fort Belknap Indian Community [3] FHQ Developments [5] Fort Peck Tribes

06

Language renewal and community knowledge

Fort Peck’s language department describes revitalization through community curriculum, Elder stories, history, songs and daily cultural learning. Its stated vision includes developing immersion education, which should be distinguished from evidence that a particular new school has already opened. Cumberland’s 2025 grammar provides a complementary reference on Nakoda sounds, grammar, kinship and writing systems, with attention to different practical orthographies. Community teaching and scholarly documentation serve related purposes, but the authority of particular speakers, families and institutions remains essential to how knowledge is learned and shared.

Read the sources [5] Fort Peck Tribes [6] University of Nebraska Press / JSTOR
